sentences.text: Genyodectes is a genus of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaur whose name means "jaw bite" in Greek.
This predator possessed relatively large and protruding premaxillary teeth similar to those of Ceratosaurus.
It differs from most theropods by having these premaxillary teeth arranged in an overlapping en-echelon pattern, a trait also found in Ceratosaurus.
Genyodectes can be distinguished from Ceratosaurus by having four premaxillary teeth instead of three.
Some estimates suggest Genyodectes could have reached a length of around 9 meters.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was collected from the Cerro Barcino Formation in the Chubut Province of Argentina.
The genus Genyodectes was described by English paleontologist Sir Arthur S. Woodward in 1901.
The taxonomic validity of Genyodectes was strengthened after the holotype was removed from the artificial matrix in which it had been displayed for a long time.
In 2016, Genyodectes was estimated to reach a length of 6.25 meters and a weight of 790 kilograms.
Research by Rauhut (2004) concluded that Genyodectes lacks key abelisaurid and tyrannosaurid traits but possesses many neoceratosaurian characteristics.
Evidence suggests Genyodectes was phylogenetically closer to Ceratosaurus than to more derived abelisaurs.
Rauhut (2004) concluded the Genyodectes holotype was likely collected from the Cerro Castaño Member of the Cerro Barcino Formation during the Aptian to Albian stages.
Genyodectes lived during the middle Late Cretaceous, approximately 112 million years ago in the Albian stage, in what is now South America.
The time range for Genyodectes is recorded as the Albian stage, between 113.2 and 100.5 million years ago.
Over the last decade, the classification of Genyodectes has been debated, with it being referred to variously as a megalosaurid, tyrannosaurid, Theropoda incertae sedis, or a possible abelisaurid.
